name: valve surgery overview
title: Valve surgery decision chart: leaky (regurgitant) valves are repaired where possible, tight (stenotic) valves are replaced; severe aortic stenosis is replaced surgically when the patient will live more than 5 to 7 years or by transcatheter implantation in elderly moderate-to-high-risk patients; a replacement valve is mechanical (durable, lifelong anticoagulation) or bioprosthetic (no anticoagulation, wears out in about 15 years), chosen by age, anticoagulation risk and conditions that wear tissue valves out

root.title: A valve needs surgery (WHEN: see the VALVULAR HEART DISEASE chart): REPAIR or REPLACE, and WITH WHAT?
lines: LEAKY (regurgitant) → REPAIR · TIGHT (stenotic: calcific aortic, rheumatic mitral) → must be REPLACED
the best valve is your own: every prosthesis can deteriorate, leak, clot or get infected

groups.title: SEVERE AORTIC STENOSIS: which ROUTE?
lines: no medical therapy; untreated, survival is poor

groups.title: REPLACING: which PROSTHESIS?
lines: age, bleeding risk, and what wears tissue out

head: h
Valve REPAIR
resection, neochordae, annular band; aortic root: valve-sparing
use: • operate EARLY, before New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III–IV
gain: • more valve area than a prosthesis
cost: Not for stenotic, unrepairable or endocarditis-destroyed valves

head: h
Surgical replacement (SAVR)
sternotomy or minimally invasive
use: Sternotomy if other work is needed
cost: 4–5 days in hospital, 1 month at home

head: h
Transcatheter implantation (TAVI)
femoral artery, under fluoroscopy + echo
use: e.g. 80 years with calcific AS: standard of care

head: h
MECHANICAL valve
bileaflet carbon (St Jude, On-X)
use: e.g. 55 with a bicuspid valve (or a Ross procedure)
cost: NOT if anticoagulation is a problem
